title: Human CD46 humanized mice reveal interferon associated pulmonary immune remodeling during human adenovirus type 7 lung infection

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand the mechanisms linking human adenovirus type 7 (HAdV-7) infection to pulmonary immune remodeling and lung pathology in children, addressing the limitations of current animal models.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used human CD46 (hCD46) humanized mice to evaluate pulmonary viral burden, recoverable infectious virus, and lung pathology after HAdV-7 infection, with analysis performed on lung tissues and systemic immune programs.
analysis.methods: Human CD46 humanized mice were generated and infected with HAdV-7. Pulmonary viral burden, recoverable infectious virus, and lung pathology were assessed. Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on lung tissues to characterize cellular composition, transcriptional states, and intercellular communication. Systemic relevance was further analyzed using human PBMC transcriptomes.
analysis.main_results: hCD46 humanized mice showed increased pulmonary viral burden, recoverable infectious virions, and more severe lung pathology after HAdV-7 infection. Single-cell profiling revealed depletion of resident alveolar macrophages, expansion of inflammatory macrophage subsets, and remodeling of lymphoid transcriptional states. These changes were accompanied by prominent type I/II interferon and interferon-associated chemokine programs. B cells and CD4+ and CD8+ T cells showed ISGs associated transcriptional states, with alterations in selected effector- and memory-associated programs.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study concluded that HAdV-7 infection in hCD46 humanized mice was associated with an interferon-enriched pulmonary inflammatory environment, prominent inflammatory myeloid remodeling, and altered lymphoid transcriptional states, providing a useful model for studying HAdV-7 associated lung disease and preclinical evaluation of antiviral, immunomodulatory, and vaccine strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that the hCD46 humanized mouse model can be used to study HAdV-7 associated lung disease and to evaluate antiviral, immunomodulatory, and vaccine strategies, enhancing our understanding of the disease mechanisms and potential therapeutic interventions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study design limitations include the use of a specific humanized mouse model, which may not fully recapitulate all aspects of human HAdV-7 infection. The evidence strength is moderate due to the reliance on a single model system and the need for further validation in human studies.

analysis.summary_en: This study used human CD46 humanized mice to evaluate HAdV-7 infection, showing increased pulmonary viral burden, interferon-enriched inflammation, and immune cell remodeling. The findings suggest a useful model for studying HAdV-7 associated lung disease and evaluating therapeutic strategies.

analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings can improve our understanding of adenoviral infection mechanisms and may contribute toward developing novel antiviral strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings may contribute toward developing novel antiviral strategies and improve our understanding of adenoviral infection mechanisms.

title: Porcine Adenovirus-Based Viral Vectors for Swine Vaccines: A Scoping Review and Future Perspectives

analysis.scope_and_question: This review summarizes current knowledge on PAdV biology, vector engineering, vaccine applications, immune responses, translational challenges, and future priorities.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: Early studies showed that recombinant PAdV vectors can express heterologous antigens from important swine pathogens, including classical swine fever virus, pseudorabies virus, and transmissible gastroenteritis virus.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Compared with human adenovirus-based vectors, PAdV vectors may offer potential advantages in host association, veterinary relevance, and mucosal delivery while avoiding direct reliance on common human adenovirus backbones.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Major gaps remain in anti-PAdV immunity, genetic stability, biosafety, shedding, target-animal safety, DIVA compatibility, manufacturing, and regulatory readiness.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Comparative adenovirus-vectored swine vaccine studies support the broader feasibility of adenoviral antigen delivery for porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome, porcine epidemic diarrhea, swine influenza, and African swine fever, but these data should not be interpreted as direct validation of PAdV for these diseases.

analysis.summary_en: This review summarizes current knowledge on PAdV biology, vector engineering, vaccine applications, immune responses, translational challenges, and future priorities. Early studies showed that recombinant PAdV vectors can express heterologous antigens from important swine pathogens, including classical swine fever virus, pseudorabies virus, and transmissible gastroenteritis virus. Compared with human adenovirus-based vectors, PAdV vectors may offer potential advantages in host association, veterinary relevance, and mucosal delivery while avoiding direct reliance on common human adenovirus backbones. Major gaps remain in anti-PAdV immunity, genetic stability, biosafety, shedding, target-animal safety, DIVA compatibility, manufacturing, and regulatory readiness. Comparative adenovirus-vectored swine vaccine studies support the broader feasibility of adenoviral antigen delivery for porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome, porcine epidemic diarrhea, swine influenza, and African swine fever, but these data should not be interpreted as direct validation of PAdV for these diseases.

title: Targeting of Immune Cells by Human Adenoviruses: CD46 Receptor Density Influences Entry of Chimaeric Ad5F35 into Natural Killer Cells

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate how the density of the CD46 receptor influences the entry of chimaeric Ad5F35 virus into natural killer cells, addressing the gap in understanding the relationship between receptor density and viral transduction efficiency.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved a comparison of different adenovirus receptors using transcriptomic and proteomic databases, and tested the transduction efficiency of Ad5F35 in primary human NK cells and A549 epithelial cells.
analysis.methods: The researchers utilized a hybrid virus, Ad5F35, which incorporates the Ad35 fibre into the Ad5 genome, and employed RNA interference to reduce CD46 density in HeLa cells, enabling a direct comparison of transduction efficiency across cell types.
analysis.main_results: Lymphocytes required approximately 10-to-20-fold more Ad5F35 particles per cell compared to A549 epithelial cells to achieve similar transduction levels. Quantitation showed that primary NK cells had approximately 100 CD46 molecules per μm2, while HeLa cells had approximately 2000 CD46 per μm2, indicating a 20-fold difference.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate that CD46 receptor density is a critical factor in determining the efficiency of Ad5F35 transduction, highlighting the importance of receptor density in viral entry mechanisms.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results have implications for the development of adenoviral vectors for gene delivery in primary human NK cells, potentially improving the efficacy of gene therapy applications targeting these cells.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on transcriptomic and proteomic databases and the use of RNA interference to manipulate CD46 density, which may not fully represent in vivo conditions. The evidence is moderate in strength due to these constraints.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates how the density of the CD46 receptor influences the transduction efficiency of the chimaeric Ad5F35 virus in primary human NK cells compared to A549 epithelial cells. The results highlight CD46 density as a critical determinant of Ad5F35 entry and suggest its potential utility in gene delivery applications targeting NK cells. However, the study's reliance on databases and RNA interference introduces limitations, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

title: A novel adenovirus 19K/IX protein enhances infection by attenuating proteasomal degradation of tyrosine-ubiquitinated capsid protein IX

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the function of a newly identified alternatively spliced viral transcript, 19K/IX, in human adenoviruses (HAdVs), which are clinically important pathogens causing a wide range of diseases. The research addresses the need to understand how HAdVs use alternative splicing to expand their coding capacity and regulate gene expression during infection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used replication-competent epitope-tagged HAdV-C5 viruses to investigate the function of the 19K/IX protein. The research was conducted in vitro, focusing on the interaction between the 19K/IX protein and the minor capsid protein IX (pIX) in HAdV-C5 infection.
analysis.methods: They demonstrated that the 19K/IX protein binds to and stabilizes pIX, thereby attenuating its proteasomal degradation and enhancing the production of infectious viral progeny. The study involved molecular biology techniques, including protein-protein interaction assays and ubiquitination analysis.
analysis.main_results: Mechanistically, pIX degradation is mediated by non-canonical ubiquitination of conserved tyrosine residues Y14 and Y49, which confer pIX subnuclear localization and partially mediate its interaction with the PSMC3 subunit of the 26S proteasome.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study identifies 19K/IX as a novel regulator of HAdV-C5 infection and suggests that non-canonical tyrosine ubiquitination contributes to the regulation of capsid protein IX stability. This finding deepens our understanding of HAdV-C5 gene regulation and protein homeostasis and highlights the functional importance of non-canonical HAdV transcripts.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that non-canonical tyrosine ubiquitination plays a role in the regulation of capsid protein IX stability, which could have implications for understanding HAdV-C5 infection and potentially for developing therapeutic strategies against HAdV infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its in vitro nature and the focus on HAdV-C5, which may not fully represent the behavior of other HAdV species. The evidence strength is moderate due to the limited scope of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the function of the 19K/IX protein in human adenoviruses (HAdVs) and found that it stabilizes the minor capsid protein IX, enhancing viral production. title: Polyclonal breast milk–derived secretory IgA confers broad antiviral protection against multiple respiratory viruses

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address limitations in current antiviral protection methods by testing LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation derived from pooled human breast milk, against clinically relevant respiratory viruses. The research sought to understand the broad antiviral activity of LCTG-001 against viruses such as respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved the collection and purification of LCTG-001 from the breast milk of 120 lactating individuals. Neutrophils were isolated from peripheral blood of healthy donors, and various cell lines including A549, HEK 293T, MDCK, and Hep-2 cells were maintained under specific conditions for virus infection studies.
analysis.methods: LCTG-001 was purified and pooled from breast milk, and its concentration was determined using a spectrophotometer. SDS–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis was performed to assess the protein content. Neutrophils were isolated using density gradient centrifugation. Viruses were infected into cell lines, and LCTG-001 was preincubated with viruses before infection. Neutralization titers were determined by measuring the highest antibody dilution that achieved a 50% reduction in fluorescence compared to the virus control wells.
analysis.main_results: LCTG-001 demonstrated broad antiviral activity against respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that LCTG-001's broad antiviral activity against multiple respiratory viruses suggests its potential as a protective agent against these pathogens.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings could inform the development of new antiviral strategies and provide insights into the use of secretory IgA for respiratory virus protection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the use of cell lines and the need for further in vivo studies to confirm the findings. The evidence strength is moderate due to the in vitro nature of the experiments.

analysis.summary_en: This study tested LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation from breast milk, against respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus. LCTG-001 demonstrated broad antiviral activity, suggesting its potential as a protective agent against these pathogens.

title: Highly neutralizing anti–IFN-ω autoantibodies underlie severe pediatric adenovirus infection

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the role of anti–IFN-ω autoantibodies in severe pediatric adenovirus infection, addressing the gap in understanding how these antibodies might contribute to disease severity by impairing antiviral defenses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved children with adenovirus infection, including the index patient, and healthy controls. Plasma and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were collected from these participants for analysis.
analysis.methods: The researchers used ELISA to measure IFN-α and IFN-ω levels in plasma, qPCR to assess mRNA levels in cell cultures, and a luciferase reporter assay to evaluate IFN signaling. They also performed viral cultures and CCK-8 assays to measure virus-induced cytotoxicity.
analysis.main_results: Functional assays showed that the patient’s plasma strongly neutralized IFN-ω, leading to high adenovirus replication and cytotoxicity. Multiplex real-time PCR revealed a progressive increase in adenovirus DNA levels, indicating systemic spread. No other viral infections were detected in the samples.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that neutralizing anti–IFN-ω autoantibodies may reduce IFN-ω bioavailability, thereby impairing its antiviral defense mechanisms during adenoviral infection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results highlight the potential role of autoantibodies in modulating immune responses to adenovirus, which could inform future diagnostic approaches and therapeutic strategies for severe adenovirus infections in children.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its focus on a single patient and the lack of a larger cohort, which may affect generalizability. However, the evidence is supported by direct functional assays and molecular measurements, providing a moderate level of confidence.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the role of anti–IFN-ω autoantibodies in severe pediatric adenovirus infection. It reports that the patient’s plasma strongly neutralized IFN-ω, impairing its antiviral signaling and leading to high virus replication and cytotoxicity. Methods included ELISA, qPCR, and luciferase reporter assays to assess IFN levels and signaling. Results showed a progressive rise in adenovirus DNA levels in plasma, indicating systemic dissemination, and no evidence of other viral infections. The authors interpret these findings as suggesting that neutralizing anti–IFN-ω autoantibodies may compromise antiviral defenses. The study has moderate confidence due to its focus on a single patient and limited sample size, though the evidence is grounded in direct functional and molecular analyses. These results could inform future research on immune modulation in adenovirus infections and guide diagnostic or therapeutic strategies for severe cases in children.
